newsitem.title: FRANCE: Former HK governor Patten denies leaking secrets.
newsitem.headline: Former HK governor Patten denies leaking secrets.

text.p: Former Hong Kong governor Chris Patten on Monday denied allegations that he leaked details of a secret British deal with China.
"Allegations made about this article are without foundation," Patten told Reuters, referring to a British newspaper report.
"I stand on my record. I left Hong Kong in extremely good condition," he said during a brief interview at his new home in southwestern France.

Britain's new Labour government on Sunday confirmed press reports that authorities were investigating allegations that Patten, Hong Kong's last British governor, leaked secret documents to writer and broadcaster Jonathan Dimbleby.
"That will be done in a proper, objective and authoritative way," minister without portfolio Peter Mandelson said of the investigation.

The Sunday Times said Patten was being investigated by British authorities and could be prosecuted for allegedly leaking details of a secret British deal with China in the 1980s over the future of Hong Kong.

Patten left Hong Kong when it was handed back to China at the end of June after 156 years of colonial rule. He is now staying in Saint Martin-Laguepie but plans to travel to London "in a few days", he told Reuters.
The Sunday Times said the investigation was sparked by its publication of extracts from Dimbleby's recently published book on Patten's time in office.
Patten was said to have been angry at Britain's failure to bring in direct elections in Hong Kong from 1988 in order to hand over a democratic administration to China.
Dimbleby has refused to divulge information about his sources.
In London, former British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Monday he did not think ministry officials were out to get Patten.

"The Foreign Office, like the civil service as a whole, are absolutely loyal to the government of the day and I don't believe they would allow any personal views of that kind to colour the way in which they carried out their responsibilities," Rifkind, the Conservative foreign secretary until May, told BBC radio.

"For two years I handled Hong Kong policy as foreign secretary and I regularly discussed these issues with my advisers ... Some of them may have had their personal views but I got nothing but absolutely loyal support for the policy which was the policy of the government," he added.
